sources.headline: Mushroom murderer fails to overturn convictions in Australian court challenge
sources.text: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said."We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

sources.headline: Erin Patterson to die in prison after losing appeal against mushroom murder convictions
sources.text: Erin Patterson has lost her bid to overturn her convictions and been resentenced to life behind bars with no chance of release, as Victoria’s highest court handed down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.The court of appeal ruled on the two appeals on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.Patterson, 52, did not attend the 15-minute court hearing in person, and showed no emotion on the video feed as McLeish outlined why her appeal had failed, and how the director of public prosecutions had succeeded in seeking a longer sentence.Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailShe was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.McLeish said the court had granted leave to appeal on the first two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, but dismissed the appeal, and dismissed the five other grounds raised by her lawyers.He said the court granted the DPP appeal against the sentence, however, as it was clear the original sentence did not properly reflect the seriousness of her offending.Erin Patterson appeal: judges reject mushroom murderer’s bid to overturn sentencing - videoMcLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”.The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms.“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said.When the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, and walked off-screen.In the courtroom, family members hugged and were emotional, and detectives involved in the case looked elated. Nobody commented outside court.A visual guide to people involved in the storyPatterson now must apply to the high court for leave to appeal, should she wish to continue fighting her conviction or new sentence.She is one of only a handful of Victorian offenders sentenced to life without parole, and one of the only women in Australian history to be given the sentence.Written reasons for the decision were provided to media later on Friday.In them, the court said while the first ground of the DPP’s appeal – that trial judge erred in finding that there was a substantial chance Patterson would be in solitary confinement for much of her sentence – had failed, it was clear the second ground, that the sentence was manifestly inadequate, should succeed.The court found they were “heinous crimes” and “we are driven to conclude that a non-parole period of 33 years fails to reflect the calculated criminality of the applicant in committing three murders and attempting a fourth”.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of the applicant’s extended family,” the court found.“The taking of three lives (and the attempt on another) in these circumstances called in our view for much stronger denunciation.”In relation to Patterson’s appeal, the court described many of the grounds as having no substance, being without merit, or even fanciful.In relation to the ground that the sequestering of the jury in the same hotel as the police informant and members of the prosecution amounted to a substantial miscarriage of justice, the court found that it “was plainly unfortunate that [the] situation arose”. It said it was “highly undesirable” and “the judge would not have countenanced this arrangement if approval for it had been sought in advance”.But the justices said there was no evidence any wrongdoing had occurred.“The accommodation arrangements offered fertile grounds for speculation but no objective basis for the fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function of rendering a verdict according to law. “In relation to ground two – that undue weight was placed on evidence given by a telecommunications expert that raised the possibility she visited two sites where death cap mushrooms had been reported – the court found the probative value of the evidence was not outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice to Patterson.In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.Richard Edney, for Patterson, had said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.Erin Patterson: Australia’s mushroom murderer sentenced to life in prison – video“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.

sources.headline: Court Rejects Erin Patterson’s Appeal in Mushroom Murders Case
sources.text: Judges took away the possibility of parole for an Australian woman, Erin Patterson, and rejected a bid to overturn her conviction over a deadly beef Wellington lunch.

sources.headline: Erin Patterson one of few Australians sentenced to die in prison
sources.text: On Friday, Victoria's Court of Appeal ruled Erin Patterson will spend the rest of her life behind bars with no chance of parole.WARNING: The following story contains graphic details that may distress some readers.A life sentence with no parole is a sentence rarely handed down in Australia, with only a handful of people across the country's prisons currently serving such a sentence. In a country with no death penalty, it is the harshest punishment our criminal justice system can hand down to a convicted person.Many of Victoria's most notorious killers, including Adrian Bayley and Jaymes Todd were sentenced to life in prison, but had non-parole periods affixed to their sentences, leaving the door open to eventual freedom.But Justice Stephen McLeish said Patterson's offending was "extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms".Patterson was arrested at her Leongatha home in November 2023. (ABC News)Former criminal barrister Christopher Corns described the sentencing as "an exceptionally rare event"."[There is] a very strong presumption that even in a case of murder, where a head sentence of life is imposed, then a non-parole period must be set. This is exactly what the sentencing judge did in Patterson's case," he said."There have only been three [or] four cases where a court in Victoria has refused to set a non-parole period where the head sentence was life."Dr Corns said he could not think of any other case where the Victorian Court of Appeal had re-sentenced someone and arrived at a non-parole period.Erin Patterson's re-sentencing thus puts her in a rare grouping of convicted killers in Australia who will never be eligible for parole.Michael CardamoneMichael Cardamone is currently serving a life sentence without parole for the murder of his neighbour Karen Chetcuti near Wangaratta in 2016.Michael Cardamone was the first person in Victoria without prior murder convictions to receive a life sentence without parole. (ABC News)The murder, which involved extensive torture, was described by Justice Lex Lasry as "quite simply horrifying, depraved and disgusting", with the veteran judge saying he was shocked by the crime.A long-time methamphetamine user, Cardamone was on parole at the time of the murder for raping a 15-year-old girl. Cardamone initially tried to pin the murder on a group of fictional Lebanese men who he said had threatened him to stay quiet, before later attempting to shift blame to a friend who had unwittingly helped him set fire to Ms Chetcuti's car.He later attempted to have the friend murdered to prevent him from giving evidence at trial.Peter DupasOne of Victoria's most notorious serial killers, Peter Dupas is serving multiple life sentences over the murder and mutilation of several women in the late 1990s. Serial killer Peter Dupas has been in prison for more than two decades. (Joe Castro: AAP)Dupas served multiple prison sentences from the 1970s to the 1990s for attacks on women.Nicole Patterson, 28, was killed at her Melbourne home on April 19, 1999 and Margaret Maher's partially-clothed body was found on October 4, 1997.In 2008, Dupas was found guilty of the murder of Mersina Halgavis, but that conviction was later overturned by the Court of Appeal and a retrial ordered. A second jury convicted him again."At a fundamental level, you present for us, the awful, threatening and unanswerable question: how did you become to be as you are?" Justice Elizabeth Hollingworth asked during his sentencing."You will now live out the rest of your days in prison."Paul HaighSerial killer Paul Haigh is currently serving six life sentences for a series of murders in the 1970s, and a prison murder in 1991. Serial killer Paul Haigh, in a photo taken circa 1974. (gallery.skcentral.com)In 1979, Haigh murdered his friend Wayne Keith Smith, along with Mr Smith's ex-girlfriend Sheryle Ann Gardner and her 10-year-old son Danny Mitchell.The same year, he stabbed his 19-year-old girlfriend Lisa Maude Brearley 157 times.While in prison, Haigh confessed to the 1978 murders of Tattslotto agency worker Evelyn Adams and pizza shop worker Bruno Cingolani.He was also convicted of hanging fellow Pentridge inmate Donald Hatherley in 1991, but argued it was an assisted suicide.In 2009, Supreme Court Justice Betty King ordered Haigh never be released.Haigh applied to the Victorian Supreme Court in 2012 to be given a minimum jail term, but was denied.Katherine Mary KnightFormer meatworker Katherine Mary Knight became infamous after becoming the first Australian woman to be sentenced to life in prison without parole. Katherine Knight (right) pictured with and her partner and eventual victim John Price. (AAP: Random House/PR)In 2000, Knight skinned and beheaded her partner John Price at his home in the NSW town of Aberdeen.She then cooked parts of Mr Price's body in the oven, and arranged them on plates she left as meals for his son and daughter.Justice Barry O'Keefe said at the time that "a crime of the kind committed by the prisoner calls for the maximum penalty the law empowers the court to impose".Knight's file is marked "never to be released".

sources.headline: Woman jailed for mushroom poison murders given harsher sentence
sources.text:
October 30, 2026 / 8:31 AM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
An Australian appeals court on Friday ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the "shocking criminality" involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband's relatives with death cap mushrooms. The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson's appeal of her convictions and upheld prosecutors' challenge to the leniency of her 33-year nonparole sentence, meaning she will spend the rest of her life behind bars. Beforehand, she would have been 82 years old when she could be considered for release. "Extraordinarily cold and calculated""This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of all three judges. "In all the circumstances after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period," McLeish added. Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be imprisoned for life without possibility of parole. The first is meatworker Katherine Knight, who was sentenced in New South Wales state in 2001 for the murder a year earlier of her partner John Price, whom she'd stabbed at least 37 times. Patterson's convictions stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.
Erin Patterson arrives at the Supreme Court of Victoria in Melbourne, Australia, Monday, Aug. 25, 2025.
Jason Edwards/AAP Image, POOL via AP, File
She can apply to Australia's High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option.
Patterson insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the beef Wellington pastry dishes accidentally.Death caps are responsible for 90% of lethal mushroom poisoning globally, the BBC reported.In 2022, doctors in Massachusetts were able to save a mother and son who nearly died from death cap mushroom poisoning. In 2020, a spate of poisonings in Victoria, Australia, killed one person and hospitalized seven others. She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder.
Murders attract global attentionThe deaths of Patterson's parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, within days of having lunch immediately attracted an extraordinary level of global media attention.The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations. Emmy-nominated actor Melanie Lynskey announced this week she will star as Erin Patterson in a six-episode series for the subscription video-on-demand streaming service Paramount+. Lynskey is also executive producer of the series that dramatizes the 97 days from the fatal lunch until Patterson's arrest. Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson survived the lunch after spending weeks in the hospital. Erin Patterson was convicted of his attempted murder. Prosecutors argued at an appeal hearing in August that she should never become eligible for parole. They argued the minimum period behind bars did not reflect the "calculated criminality" of the case.
McLeish said Patterson's intent to murder all four was sustained for almost three weeks from when she invited them to lunch. Her crimes involved an "elaborate series of deceptions" including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absences of her two children from the lunch, the judge said. The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Erin Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis. Wilkinson, a Baptist pastor, also testified about the grief after his wife died from the poisoning.
Ian Wilkinson departs the Latrobe Valley Magistrates Court in Morwell, Australia, on Wednesday, June 4, 2025, during a break in the trial of a woman accused of his attempted murder.
James Ross/AAP Image via AP
"I only feel half alive without her," Wilkinson said at the trial before weeping.Patterson allegedly destroyed evidenceMcLeish noted Erin Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from. "The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust," McLeish said. Patterson opted not to attend court and watched the verdicts by video link from prison.
Because of her notoriety, Patterson is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne's Dame Phyllis Frost Centre women's prison. The unit is for prisoners assessed as being at high risk from other inmates. In sentencing her in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Bale said there was a "substantial chance" that Patterson could be held in "solitary confinement for years to come." Patterson's estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was invited to the lunch but declined the day before. After her conviction, pretrial evidence was released that detailed the husband's suspicion that Erin Patterson had previously attempted to kill him. Simon Patterson testified at a pretrial hearing that he had declined the lunch invitation out of fear.

Published: 8:41am, 30 Oct 2026
Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson lost a bid to overturn her convictions and had a harsher sentence imposed on Friday, failing to prove she was wrongfully jailed for killing three people with a poisoned lunch.

Patterson was found guilty last year of murdering her husband’s parents and elderly aunt, deliberately lacing their beef Wellington meal with highly toxic death cap mushrooms.

The 52-year-old maintained her triple murder convictions were a “miscarriage of justice”, urging the Court of Appeal in Victoria state to either set her free or have the case heard again.

The court found the killings were “carefully planned and deliberate” and there were insufficient grounds to try the case again.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated,” judge Stephen McLeish said.

“It stands to be denounced in the strongest terms.”

Patterson has also been convicted of the attempted murder of her husband’s uncle, a small-town local pastor who survived after weeks in hospital.

The court not only threw out Patterson’s appeal, but also found that her original jail sentence did not match the gravity of her crimes.

Patterson was initially eligible to apply for release after 33 years.

The court ruled that she should not be eligible for parole, meaning Patterson is likely to die in prison.

03:26
Australia’s ‘mushroom murderer’ found guilty of killing in-laws in shocking poison plot

Patterson did not front the trial in person, instead watching proceedings via video link from a maximum-security prison on the outskirts of Melbourne.

Her lawyers had alleged a litany of irregularities in the trial, including an “oppressive” cross-examination and unfair decisions on the admission of evidence.

Prosecutors argued that the non-parole period of 33 years imposed by the judge was “manifestly inadequate”.

They said the judge erred in finding there was a substantial chance Patterson would be held in solitary confinement for years to come and this “infected” his decision on parole.

Patterson’s trial last year drew podcasters, film crews and true crime fans to a courthouse in the rural town of Morwell, a sedate hamlet in Victoria better known for its prize-winning roses.

Audiences from New York to New Delhi followed every twist of what many now simply call the “mushroom murders”.

The motive of the killings remains a mystery.

A 12-person jury found Patterson guilty in July last year of murdering her husband Simon’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, as well as his aunt, Heather Wilkinson, at her home in the Victorian farming village of Leongatha.

She was also found guilty of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian, a pastor who fell gravely ill but eventually recovered.

sources.headline: Mushroom killer must never be released from prison, court says
sources.text: A court has ruled that an Australian woman who murdered three people by serving them beef wellington laced with poisonous mushrooms can never be released from prison.
